claims.text: The baseline alloy is Ti65(AlCrNbV) without Zr.
The conventionally rolled baseline has a coarse, solid-solution microstructure.
Approximately 7 at% Zr is to be incorporated into Ti65(AlCrNbV).
The proposed processing route comprises casting, 50% hot rolling, 70% cold rolling, and rapid annealing at about 850°C for 30–50 seconds.
Adding Zr and applying the proposed processing route will produce a uniform dispersion of nanoscale Zr-induced precipitates.
Zr addition will enhance lattice distortion because Zr has a larger atomic radius than the relevant matrix constituents.
Zr-induced lattice strain will strengthen the alloy through solid-solution strengthening.
The proposed thermomechanical processing conditions will promote controlled nucleation and growth of nanoscale precipitates.
The nanoscale precipitates will impede dislocation motion.
Solid-solution strain and precipitation strengthening will specifically reinforce high-temperature yield strength.
The modified alloy will have approximately 20% greater high-temperature specific yield strength than the stated baseline.
The anticipated strength improvement will hold at approximately 800–900°C under tensile or creep loading.
The Zr-modified alloy will retain excellent room-temperature ductility.
The Zr-modified alloy will retain a low density near 5 g/cm³.
The proposed Zr addition will not add significant mass relative to the baseline.
Precipitate coarsening or heterogeneous precipitate distribution may reduce the expected high-temperature strength improvement.
The magnitude of the predicted improvement depends on the processing–structure relationship and may differ from 20%.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant 15–20% high-temperature yield-strength improvement relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe the intended nanoscale precipitate structure would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline lacks both Zr and the optimized rapid-annealing treatment, whereas the experimental control receives the same rapid annealing as the Zr-modified alloy. Thus, the decisive experiment uses a different baseline and isolates Zr addition rather than testing the full combined intervention against the stated baseline.
